claim: ISRIB substantially reversed the translational effects elicited by phosphorylation of eIF2α.

claim: ISRIB induced no major changes in translation or mRNA levels in unstressed cells.
source: ISRIB substantially reversed the translational effects elicited by phosphorylation of eIF2α and induced no major changes in translation or mRNA levels in unstressed cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data from ISRIB-treated unstressed cells.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation-induced stress granule (SG) formation was blocked by ISRIB.
source: eIF2α phosphorylation-induced stress granule (SG) formation was blocked by ISRIB.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live cell imaging data showing reduced SG formation with ISRIB treatment.

claim: ISRIB addition to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs induced their rapid disassembly.
source: Strikingly, ISRIB addition to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs induced their rapid disassembly, liberating mRNAs into the actively translating pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data showing SG disassembly within 5 minutes of ISRIB addition.

claim: ISRIB addition to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs liberated mRNAs into the actively translating pool.
source: Strikingly, ISRIB addition to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs induced their rapid disassembly, liberating mRNAs into the actively translating pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation data showing restored translation after ISRIB addition.

claim: Restoration of mRNA translation and modulation of SG dynamics may be an effective treatment of neurodegenerative diseases characterized by eIF2α phosphorylation, SG formation, and cognitive loss.
source: Restoration of mRNA translation and modulation of SG dynamics may be an effective treatment of neurodegenerative diseases characterized by eIF2α phosphorylation, SG formation, and cognitive loss.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed effects of ISRIB on translation and SG dynamics.

claim: The ISR is mediated by diverse stress-sensing kinases that converge on a common target, serine 51 in eukaryotic translation initiation factor alpha (eIF2α).
source: The ISR is mediated by diverse stress-sensing kinases that converge on a common target, serine 51 in eukaryotic translation initiation factor alpha (eIF2α) eliciting both global and gene-specific translational effects (Harding et al., 2003; Wek et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Harding et al., 2003; Wek et al., 2006).

claim: Mammalian genomes encode four eIF2α kinases: PERK, GCN2, PKR, and HRI.

evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about HRI activation.

claim: The eIF2α kinase PERK is part of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: The eIF2α kinase PERK is also part of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the UPR.

claim: The UPR is comprised of three ER-localized transmembrane sensors: IRE1, ATF6, and PERK.
source: This intracellular stress signaling network is comprised of three ER-localized transmembrane sensors, IRE1, ATF6, and PERK, which initiate unique signaling cascades upon sensing an increase in unfolded proteins in the ER lumen (Walter and Ron, 2011; Pavitt and Ron, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Walter and Ron, 2011; Pavitt and Ron, 2012).

claim: eIF2α is a subunit of an essential translation initiation factor conserved throughout eukaryotes and archaea.
source: The common mediator of the ISR, eIF2α, is a subunit of an essential translation initiation factor conserved throughout eukaryotes and archaea.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2α.

claim: The heterotrimeric eIF2 complex is composed of subunits α, β and γ.
source: The heterotrimeric eIF2 complex (composed of subunits α, β and γ) brings initiator methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) to translation initiation complexes and mediates start codon recognition.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2 structure.

claim: The eIF2 complex brings initiator methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) to translation initiation complexes.
source: The heterotrimeric eIF2 complex (composed of subunits α, β and γ) brings initiator methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) to translation initiation complexes and mediates start codon recognition.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2 function.

claim: The eIF2 complex mediates start codon recognition.
source: The heterotrimeric eIF2 complex (composed of subunits α, β and γ) brings initiator methionyl tRNA (Met-tRNAi) to translation initiation complexes and mediates start codon recognition.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2 function.

claim: eIF2 binds GTP along with Met-tRNAi to form a ternary complex (eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi).
source: It binds GTP along with Met-tRNAi to form a ternary complex (eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi) that assembles, along with the 40S ribosomal subunit and several other initiation factors, into the 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ternary complex formation.

claim: The ternary complex assembles with the 40S ribosomal subunit and several other initiation factors into the 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC).
source: It binds GTP along with Met-tRNAi to form a ternary complex (eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi) that assembles, along with the 40S ribosomal subunit and several other initiation factors, into the 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about PIC assembly.

claim: The 43S PIC is recruited to the 5′ methylguanine cap of an mRNA and scans the 5′UTR for an AUG initiation codon.
source: The 43S PIC is recruited to the 5′ methylguanine cap of an mRNA and scans the 5′UTR for an AUG initiation codon (Hinnebusch and Lorsch, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Hinnebusch and Lorsch, 2012).

claim: Start site codon recognition triggers GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
source: Start site codon recognition triggers GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release, which is followed by release of eIF2 from the 40S subunit, allowing binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to join.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release is followed by release of eIF2 from the 40S subunit.
source: Start site codon recognition triggers GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release, which is followed by release of eIF2 from the 40S subunit, allowing binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to join.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: Release of eIF2 from the 40S subunit allows binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to join.
source: Start site codon recognition triggers GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release, which is followed by release of eIF2 from the 40S subunit, allowing binding of the 60S ribosomal subunit to join.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: After 60S ribosomal subunit joining, the elongation phase of protein synthesis ensues.
source: After these events, the elongation phase of protein synthesis ensues.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about translation.

claim: To engage in a new round of initiation, the newly released eIF2 complex has to be re-loaded with GTP.
source: To engage in a new round of initiation, the newly released eIF2 complex has to be re-loaded with GTP, a reaction catalyzed by its dedicated guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), the heteropentameric eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2 recycling.

claim: GTP re-loading of eIF2 is catalyzed by eIF2B, a heteropentameric guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF).
source: To engage in a new round of initiation, the newly released eIF2 complex has to be re-loaded with GTP, a reaction catalyzed by its dedicated guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), the heteropentameric eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2B function.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α does not directly affect its function in the PIC.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α does not directly affect its function in the PIC, but rather inhibits eIF2B, thereby depleting ternary complex and reducing translation initiation (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2001).

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α inhibits eIF2B, thereby depleting ternary complex and reducing translation initiation.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α does not directly affect its function in the PIC, but rather inhibits eIF2B, thereby depleting ternary complex and reducing translation initiation (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2001).

claim: eIF2B complex is limiting in cells, present in lower abundance than eIF2.
source: eIF2B complex is limiting in cells, present in lower abundance than eIF2; a small amount of phospho-eIF2α therefore acts as a competitive inhibitor with dramatic effects on eIF2B activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF2B abundance.

claim: A small amount of phospho-eIF2α acts as a competitive inhibitor with dramatic effects on eIF2B activity.
source: eIF2B complex is limiting in cells, present in lower abundance than eIF2; a small amount of phospho-eIF2α therefore acts as a competitive inhibitor with dramatic effects on eIF2B activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and logical inference from eIF2B being limiting.

claim: When eIF2B is inhibited and ternary complex is unavailable, the rate of translation initiation decreases.
source: When eIF2B is inhibited and ternary complex is unavailable, the rate of translation initiation decreases.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: Unimpaired elongation in the face of reduced initiation allows translating ribosomes to run off of their mRNAs, generating naked mRNAs.
source: Unimpaired elongation in the face of reduced initiation allows translating ribosomes to run off of their mRNAs, generating naked mRNAs that can then bind to RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and form messenger ribonucleoproteins, which can further assemble into stress granules (SGs).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about stress granule formation.

claim: Naked mRNAs can bind to RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and form messenger ribonucleoproteins, which can further assemble into stress granules (SGs).
source: Unimpaired elongation in the face of reduced initiation allows translating ribosomes to run off of their mRNAs, generating naked mRNAs that can then bind to RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and form messenger ribonucleoproteins, which can further assemble into stress granules (SGs).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about stress granule formation.

claim: Stress granules are cytoplasmic, non-membrane bounded organelles.
source: These cytoplasmic, non-membrane bounded organelles contain translationally stalled and silent mRNAs, 40S ribosomal subunits and their associated pre-initiation factors and RBPs; these RBPs facilitate the nucleation and reversible aggregation of SGs through reversible, low-affinity protein–protein interactions mediated by their low complexity domains (Buchan and Parker, 2009; Kedersha and Anderson, 2009; Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Buchan and Parker, 2009; Kedersha and Anderson, 2009; Kato et al., 2012).

claim: Stress granules contain translationally stalled and silent mRNAs, 40S ribosomal subunits and their associated pre-initiation factors and RBPs.
source: These cytoplasmic, non-membrane bounded organelles contain translationally stalled and silent mRNAs, 40S ribosomal subunits and their associated pre-initiation factors and RBPs; these RBPs facilitate the nucleation and reversible aggregation of SGs through reversible, low-affinity protein–protein interactions mediated by their low complexity domains (Buchan and Parker, 2009; Kedersha and Anderson, 2009; Kato et al., 2012).

source: Paradoxically, under conditions of reduced ternary complex formation and protein synthesis, a group of mRNAs is translationally up-regulated.

claim: mRNAs that are translationally up-regulated under ISR conditions contain short upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs.
source: These mRNAs contain short upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs, which are required for their ISR-responsive translational control (Hinnebusch, 2005; Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Hinnebusch, 2005; Jackson et al., 2010).

claim: uORFs are required for ISR-responsive translational control of target mRNAs.
source: These mRNAs contain short upstream open reading frames (uORFs) in their 5′ UTRs, which are required for their ISR-responsive translational control (Hinnebusch, 2005; Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Hinnebusch, 2005; Jackson et al., 2010).

claim: Mammalian ATF4 and CHOP are target transcripts that are translationally up-regulated under ISR conditions.
source: These target transcripts include mammalian ATF4 (a cAMP response element binding transcription factor) and CHOP (a pro-apoptotic transcription factor) (Harding et al., 2000; Vattem and Wek, 2004; Palam et al., 2011).

claim: ATF4 is a cAMP response element binding transcription factor.
source: These target transcripts include mammalian ATF4 (a cAMP response element binding transcription factor) and CHOP (a pro-apoptotic transcription factor) (Harding et al., 2000; Vattem and Wek, 2004; Palam et al., 2011).

claim: CHOP is a pro-apoptotic transcription factor.
source: These target transcripts include mammalian ATF4 (a cAMP response element binding transcription factor) and CHOP (a pro-apoptotic transcription factor) (Harding et al., 2000; Vattem and Wek, 2004; Palam et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CHOP.

claim: ATF4 regulates the transcription of many genes involved in metabolism and nutrient uptake.
source: ATF4 regulates the transcription of many genes involved in metabolism and nutrient uptake and thus is a major regulator of the transcriptional changes that ensue upon eIF2α phosphorylation and ISR induction (Harding et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Harding et al., 2003).

claim: ATF4 is a major regulator of the transcriptional changes that ensue upon eIF2α phosphorylation and ISR induction.
source: ATF4 regulates the transcription of many genes involved in metabolism and nutrient uptake and thus is a major regulator of the transcriptional changes that ensue upon eIF2α phosphorylation and ISR induction (Harding et al., 2003).

source: In animals, the ISR has been implicated in diverse processes ranging from the regulation of insulin production to learning and memory.

source: Homozygous loss of eIF2α phosphorylation leads to perinatal death but heterozygous eIF2α+/S51A animals, which have reduced levels of eIF2α phosphorylation, grow into healthy adults showing phenotypes that demonstrate the importance of translation initiation in establishment of long-term memories (Scheuner et al., 2001).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Scheuner et al., 2001).

claim: PKR−/−, GCN2−/− and eIF2α+/S51A animals display enhanced memory consolidation in learning paradigms of light training.
source: Behavioral tests demonstrated that PKR−/−, GCN2−/− and eIF2α+/S51A animals display enhanced memory consolidation in learning paradigms of light training (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2005, 2007; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2005, 2007; Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: Small molecules that modulate the ISR pathway include kinase inhibitors that target PERK or PKR.
source: Recent work identified small molecules that modulate the ISR pathway at distinct steps: (1) kinase inhibitors that target PERK or PKR (Jammi et al., 2003; Atkins et al., 2013); (2) an activator of HRI (Chen et al., 2011); (3) salubrinal, an inhibitor of eIF2α phosphatases (Boyce et al., 2005); and (4) ISRIB (Sidrauski et al., 2013).

claim: ISRIB represents the first bona fide ISR inhibitor acting downstream of all eIF2α kinases.

source: We used ribosome profiling to characterize translational changes induced by ER stress.

claim: The UPR was triggered in HEK293T cells by treating them with tunicamycin (Tm).
source: We triggered the UPR in HEK293T cells by treating them with tunicamycin (Tm), a toxin that blocks N-linked glycosylation of ER-resident proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Tunicamycin is a toxin that blocks N-linked glycosylation of ER-resident proteins.
source: We triggered the UPR in HEK293T cells by treating them with tunicamycin (Tm), a toxin that blocks N-linked glycosylation of ER-resident proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about tunicamycin.

claim: An early time point (1 hr) was analyzed to focus on translational changes preceding the extensive transcriptional induction that takes place upon activation of the three branches of the UPR.
source: We chose to analyze an early time point (1 hr) in order to focus on translational changes preceding the extensive transcriptional induction that takes place upon activation of the three branches of the UPR (for a time course of UPR induction, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 in 10.7554/eLife.00498).

claim: ATF4, ATF5, CHOP, and GADD34 mRNAs displayed significant translational upregulation upon ER stress.

evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data and a citation to established literature (Lee et al., 2012).

claim: 14% of genes in the list of ISR-translational targets contain uORFs, indicating a significant enrichment compared to 5% of non-significantly changed genes.

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: SLC35A4 is a novel uORF-containing translational target of the ISR.
source: A seventh and novel uORF-containing translational target of the ISR encodes SLC35A4, a putative nucleotide-sugar transporter (Song, 2013).

claim: SLC35A4 is a putative nucleotide-sugar transporter.
source: A seventh and novel uORF-containing translational target of the ISR encodes SLC35A4, a putative nucleotide-sugar transporter (Song, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Song, 2013).

claim: The longest uORF of SLC35A4 is translated, as peptides corresponding to the encoded polypeptide were found in a whole proteome mass spectrometry study.
source: It was recently shown that the longest uORF of SLC35A4 is indeed translated because peptides corresponding to the encoded polypeptide were found in a whole proteome mass spectrometry study (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Kim et al., 2014).

claim: Analysis of RPFs in the uORFs of the SLC35A4 and ATF4 mRNAs revealed significant ribosome density, confirming that these regulatory uORFs are normally translated.
source: Analysis of RPFs in the uORFs of the SLC35A4 and ATF4 mRNAs revealed significant ribosome density, further confirming that these regulatory uORFs are normally translated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a slight reduction in translation of mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins and translation elongation factors upon ER stress.
source: Interestingly, there was a slight reduction in translation of mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins and translation elongation factors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel A.

claim: The translation of mRNAs with a 5′ terminal oligopyrimidine (5′ TOP) motif is controlled by the activity of the mTOR kinase.
source: The translation of this functionally related class of ∼100 abundant mRNAs, which have a 5′ terminal oligopyrimidine (5′ TOP) motif, is controlled by the activity of the mTOR kinase (Meyuhas, 2000; Tang et al., 2001; Hsieh et al., 2012; Thoreen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Meyuhas, 2000; Tang et al., 2001; Hsieh et al., 2012; Thoreen et al., 2012).

claim: ER stress and eIF2α phosphorylation affects 5′ TOP translation in HEK293T cells.
source: The concerted changes that we observed in their translation upon UPR activation suggest that ER stress and eIF2α phosphorylation affects 5′ TOP translation in HEK293T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed reduction in translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs upon ER stress.

claim: ISRIB comprehensively blocked the translational changes that take place upon ER-stress.
source: As seen in Figure 1B, ISRIB comprehensively blocked the translational changes that take place upon ER-stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A large number of genes with a significant change in expression upon stress collapsed to the center of the plot with ISRIB and Tm co-treatment.
source: A large number of genes with a significant change in expression upon stress collapsed to the center of the plot with ISRIB and Tm co-treatment (Figure 1B, highlighted in black).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ISRIB abolished the induction of the known phospho-eIF2α-dependent translational targets.
source: Importantly, ISRIB abolished the induction of the known phospho-eIF2α-dependent translational targets (Figure 1B, colored pink) and the seven ISR-translational targets with previously identified uORFs (Figure 1B, colored green).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ISRIB reversed the reduction in translation of mTOR target mRNAs upon ER stress.
source: In addition, ISRIB reversed the reduction in translation of mTOR target mRNAs upon ER stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel B.

claim: ISRIB treatment alone did not have general effects on translation in non-stressed cells.
source: Importantly, ISRIB treatment alone did not have general effects on translation in non-stressed cells, as revealed by the lack of substantial changes in RPFs in most cellular mRNAs, nor did it cause any significant changes in mRNA levels (Figure 1C) and mTOR target expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, panel C.

claim: In the absence of ER stress, ISRIB-treated cells behaved like untreated cells with the exception of a reduction in the basal level of translation of ATF4 and SLC35A4 mRNAs.
source: In the absence of ER stress, ISRIB-treated cells behaved like untreated cells with the exception of a reduction in the basal level of translation of ATF4 and SLC35A4 mRNAs and a few additional mRNAs (Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ISRIB does not have global effects on translation, transcription, or mRNA stability in non-stressed cells.
source: Taken together, these data strongly support the notion that ISRIB does not have global effects on translation, transcription, or mRNA stability in non-stressed cells and underscores its remarkable ability to counteract selectively the translational changes elicited by eIF2α phosphorylation in stressed cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ribosome profiling data showing minimal changes in unstressed cells treated with ISRIB.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduction of ternary complex formation are tightly linked to the formation of stress granules (SGs).
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduction of ternary complex formation are tightly linked to the formation of stress granules (SGs) (Kedersha et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Kedersha et al., 2002).

claim: ISRIB prevents SG formation induced by thapsigargin (Tg).
source: We tested this hypothesis by inducing SG formation using thapsigargin (Tg), a potent ER stressor that inhibits the ER calcium pump and was recently shown by ribosome profiling to yield analogous translational effects to tunicamycin (Reid et al., 2014). Microscopic detection of SGs required a stronger induction of ER stress than commonly achieved with Tm, making Tg the preferred inducer. We monitored SGs by performing immunofluorescence on eIF3a, a translation initiation factor that is recruited into SGs. As expected, we found that ISRIB significantly reduced their assembly upon co-treatment with Tg (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Thapsigargin (Tg) is a potent ER stressor that inhibits the ER calcium pump.
source: We tested this hypothesis by inducing SG formation using thapsigargin (Tg), a potent ER stressor that inhibits the ER calcium pump and was recently shown by ribosome profiling to yield analogous translational effects to tunicamycin (Reid et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by a citation (Reid et al., 2014).

claim: Thapsigargin yields analogous translational effects to tunicamycin.
source: We tested this hypothesis by inducing SG formation using thapsigargin (Tg), a potent ER stressor that inhibits the ER calcium pump and was recently shown by ribosome profiling to yield analogous translational effects to tunicamycin (Reid et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Reid et al., 2014).

claim: ISRIB prevented SG formation induced by arsenite (Ars).
source: In addition, ISRIB prevented SG formation induced by arsenite (Ars), another widely used inducer of eIF2α phosphorylation via activation of HRI.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Arsenite is a widely used inducer of eIF2α phosphorylation via activation of HRI.
source: In addition, ISRIB prevented SG formation induced by arsenite (Ars), another widely used inducer of eIF2α phosphorylation via activation of HRI.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about arsenite.

claim: Both Tg and Ars treatments induced eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: As expected, both treatments induced eIF2α phosphorylation but only Tg induced the ER-resident kinase, PERK, as seen by its shift in mobility that is due to its extensive auto-phosphorylation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only Tg induced the ER-resident kinase, PERK, as seen by its shift in mobility due to extensive auto-phosphorylation.
source: As expected, both treatments induced eIF2α phosphorylation but only Tg induced the ER-resident kinase, PERK, as seen by its shift in mobility that is due to its extensive auto-phosphorylation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both the PERK mobility shift and eIF2α phosphorylation elicited by Tg treatment were blocked by a PERK inhibitor (GSK707800).
source: Both the PERK mobility shift and eIF2α phosphorylation elicited by Tg treatment were blocked by a PERK inhibitor (GSK707800; Axten et al., 2012) but not by ISRIB.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C and a citation (Axten et al., 2012).

claim: ISRIB did not block the PERK mobility shift and eIF2α phosphorylation elicited by Tg treatment.
source: Both the PERK mobility shift and eIF2α phosphorylation elicited by Tg treatment were blocked by a PERK inhibitor (GSK707800; Axten et al., 2012) but not by ISRIB.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The GSK PERK inhibitor prevented SG induction upon Tg addition.
source: Like ISRIB, and as expected by the block in eIF2α phosphorylation, the GSK PERK inhibitor prevented SG induction upon Tg addition (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SG formation can be induced in the absence of eIF2α phosphorylation by inhibiting the eIF4A helicase.
source: SG formation can also be induced in the absence of eIF2α phosphorylation by inhibiting the eIF4A helicase, which is part of the cap-binding eIF4F complex (Mazroui et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Mazroui et al., 2006).

claim: eIF4A helicase is part of the cap-binding eIF4F complex.
source: SG formation can also be induced in the absence of eIF2α phosphorylation by inhibiting the eIF4A helicase, which is part of the cap-binding eIF4F complex (Mazroui et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about eIF4A.

claim: Pateamine A (Pat A) binds to and inhibits eIF4A and blocks scanning of the PIC and translation initiation.
source: Pateamine A (Pat A) binds to and inhibits this enzyme and blocks scanning of the PIC and translation initiation (Dang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Dang et al., 2006).

claim: Pat A induced SG formation but did not cause eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: In agreement, Pat A-induced SG formation but it did not cause eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Pat-A-induced SGs were not reduced by ISRIB.
source: In contrast to phospho-eIF2α-induced SGs, Pat-A-induced SGs were not reduced by ISRIB (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: ISRIB blocks phospho-eIF2α-dependent SG induction selectively.
source: Thus, ISRIB blocks phospho-eIF2α-dependent SG induction selectively.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ISRIB blocks SGs induced by eIF2α phosphorylation but not by eIF4A inhibition.

claim: ISRIB significantly reduces SG formation driven by stresses that cause eIF2α phosphorylation (Tg and Ars) but not by phospho-eIF2α-independent induction through eIF4A inhibition (Pat A and hippuristanol [Hipp]).
source: We confirmed that in this cell line ISRIB significantly reduces SG formation driven by stresses that cause eIF2α phosphorylation (Tg and Ars) but not by phospho-eIF2α-independent induction through eIF4A inhibition (Pat A and hippuristanol [Hipp]) (Figure 3A,B) (Cencic et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B and a citation (Cencic et al., 2012).

claim: ISRIB has an EC50 of 5 nM as measured using an uORFs-ATF4-driven luciferase reporter in HEK293T cells.
source: ISRIB has an EC50 of 5 nM as previously measured using an uORFs-ATF4-driven luciferase reporter in HEK293T cells (Sidrauski et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sidrauski et al., 2013).

claim: ISRIB significantly reduced SG formation even at concentrations as low as 2 nM in U2OS cells.
source: In close agreement with the high potency measured in the reporter assay, ISRIB significantly reduced SG formation even at concentrations as low as 2 nM in U2OS cells and as expected, an inactive analog, ISRIBinact, did not reduce their formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An inactive analog of ISRIB, ISRIBinact, did not reduce SG formation.
source: In close agreement with the high potency measured in the reporter assay, ISRIB significantly reduced SG formation even at concentrations as low as 2 nM in U2OS cells and as expected, an inactive analog, ISRIBinact, did not reduce their formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of cells with CHX disassembles SGs in the presence of ongoing stress.
source: Treatment of cells with CHX disassembles SGs in the presence of ongoing stress (Kedersha et al., 2000; Mollet et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Kedersha et al., 2000; Mollet et al., 2008).

claim: SGs are highly dynamic structures with mRNAs quickly shuttling in and out.
source: This observation as well as other pharmacological and microscopy data revealed that SGs are highly dynamic structures with mRNAs quickly shuttling in and out.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about SG dynamics.

claim: When mRNAs leave SGs, translation is reinitiated; CHX then immobilizes elongating ribosomes and prevents mRNA re-entry into SGs.
source: When these mRNAs leave SGs, translation is reinitiated; CHX then immobilizes elongating ribosomes and prevents mRNA re-entry into SGs.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CHX effects on SGs.

claim: Polyribosome disassembly is blocked by CHX yet required for SG assembly, so CHX treatment dissolves pre-formed SGs.
source: Because polyribosome disassembly is blocked by CHX yet required for SG assembly, CHX treatment dissolves pre-formed SGs.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CHX effects on SGs.

claim: A 10-min treatment with CHX following Tg induction of SGs (40 min) was sufficient to observe disassembly.
source: As seen in Figure 3C, a 10-min treatment with CHX following Tg induction of SGs (40 min) was sufficient to observe disassembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ISRIB addition disassembled SGs within 10 min, even in the prolonged presence of the stressor Tg.
source: Like CHX, ISRIB addition disassembled SGs within 10 min, even in the prolonged presence of the stressor Tg (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ISRIB restored translation of mRNAs that are liberated from SGs, as seen by the quick recovery in [35S]-methionine incorporation.
source: Whereas ISRIB restored translation of mRNAs that are liberated from SGs, as seen by the quick recovery in [35S]-methionine incorporation, CHX further reduced protein synthesis (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CHX further reduced protein synthesis after SG disassembly.
source: Whereas ISRIB restored translation of mRNAs that are liberated from SGs, as seen by the quick recovery in [35S]-methionine incorporation, CHX further reduced protein synthesis (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ISRIB triggers disassembly of pre-formed SGs by loading dissociating mRNAs with actively translating ribosomes.
source: These experiments demonstrate that ISRIB triggers disassembly of pre-formed SGs by loading dissociating mRNAs with actively translating ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ISRIB disassembles SGs and restores translation.

claim: After only 5 min of ISRIB treatment, Tg-induced SGs were no longer observed in cells.
source: Strikingly, after only 5 min of ISRIB treatment, Tg-induced SGs were no longer observed in cells (Figure 3E and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3E and Video 1.

claim: P-bodies are a molecularly distinct class of RNA aggregates that serve as centers of mRNA decay.
source: We also investigated the impact of ISRIB on P-bodies, a molecularly distinct class of RNA aggregates that serve as centers of mRNA decay (Kedersha and Anderson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Kedersha and Anderson, 2009).

claim: The mRNA decay factor Dcp1 serves as a marker for P-bodies.
source: The mRNA decay factor Dcp1 serves as a marker for these structures, and we visualized them in living cells using the fusion protein Dcp1-RFP.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about P-body markers.

claim: P-bodies were constitutively present in a percentage of the cells and were not affected by ISRIB treatment or by the stressors used to induce SGs.
source: We saw that P-bodies were constitutively present in a percentage of the cells and were not affected by ISRIB treatment or by the stressors used to induce SGs over the time-course experiments explored here (Figure 3E red arrows, Video 2 and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3E and Video 2.

claim: ISRIB is the first reported antagonist of the ISR that blocks signaling downstream of all eIF2α kinases.
source: ISRIB is the first reported antagonist of the ISR that blocks signaling downstream of all eIF2α kinases.
evidence: The claim is based on the unique properties of ISRIB compared to other ISR modulators.

claim: ISRIB has good pharmacokinetic properties and brain penetration.
source: It was shown to have good pharmacokinetic properties and brain penetration, making it a useful tool to study the systemic effects of acute inhibition of the pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on prior characterization of ISRIB.

claim: ISRIB administration enhances long-term memory in rodents.
source: We showed that ISRIB administration enhances long-term memory in rodents (Sidrauski et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sidrauski et al., 2013).

claim: ISRIB blocks mGluR-mediated long-term depression (LTD) by preventing AMPAR down-regulation in the post-synaptic neuron.
source: More recently, we showed by electrical recordings in brain slices that by preventing AMPAR down-regulation in the post-synaptic neuron, ISRIB blocks mGluR-mediated long-term depression (LTD), an effect that is dependent on eIF2α phosphorylation (Di Prisco et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Di Prisco et al., 2014).

claim: mGluR-mediated LTD is dependent on eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: More recently, we showed by electrical recordings in brain slices that by preventing AMPAR down-regulation in the post-synaptic neuron, ISRIB blocks mGluR-mediated long-term depression (LTD), an effect that is dependent on eIF2α phosphorylation (Di Prisco et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Di Prisco et al., 2014).

claim: ISRIB treatment of ER-stressed cells substantially and comprehensively blocks the translational effects of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Our translational and transcriptional profiling confirmed that ISRIB treatment of ER-stressed cells substantially and comprehensively blocks the translational effects of eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ISRIB blocked SG formation that was triggered by eIF2α phosphorylation but did not abolish their assembly upon eIF4A inhibition.
source: ISRIB blocked SG formation that was triggered by eIF2α phosphorylation but did not abolish their assembly upon eIF4A inhibition; eIF4A inhibitors do not cause eIF2α phosphorylation and can induce SGs in eIF2αS51A/S51A cells (Mazroui et al., 2006; Mokas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live cell imaging data, and citations to established literature (Mazroui et al., 2006; Mokas et al., 2009).

claim: eIF4A inhibitors do not cause eIF2α phosphorylation and can induce SGs in eIF2αS51A/S51A cells.
source: ISRIB blocked SG formation that was triggered by eIF2α phosphorylation but did not abolish their assembly upon eIF4A inhibition; eIF4A inhibitors do not cause eIF2α phosphorylation and can induce SGs in eIF2αS51A/S51A cells (Mazroui et al., 2006; Mokas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Mazroui et al., 2006; Mokas et al., 2009).

claim: ISRIB solely inhibits cellular events that are a consequence of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: These data further support the notion that ISRIB solely inhibits cellular events that are a consequence of eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the selective effects of ISRIB on phospho-eIF2α-dependent processes.

claim: ISRIB does not reverse bulk translational down-regulation triggered by inhibition of CAP-dependent initiation.
source: In agreement with these observations, we previously showed by polyribosome sedimentation analysis that ISRIB does not reverse bulk translational down-regulation triggered by inhibition of CAP-dependent initiation (Sidrauski et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sidrauski et al., 2013).

claim: ISRIB is a pharmacological agent that acutely and specifically blocks the ISR.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that ISRIB is a pharmacological agent that acutely and specifically blocks the ISR and is thus an invaluable tool for in vivo studies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comprehensive data showing ISRIB's specific effects on the ISR.

claim: Almost 45% of all 5′ UTRs have at least one upstream uORF.
source: Although previous large-scale analyses have revealed that almost 45% of all 5′ UTRs have at least one upstream uORF (Calvo et al., 2009; Ingolia et al., 2011), our data revealed that only a few of these mRNAs contain uORFs with regulatory properties that significantly enhance translation of their downstream coding sequences upon eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Calvo et al., 2009; Ingolia et al., 2011).

claim: Only a few mRNAs contain uORFs with regulatory properties that significantly enhance translation of their downstream coding sequences upon eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Although previous large-scale analyses have revealed that almost 45% of all 5′ UTRs have at least one upstream uORF (Calvo et al., 2009; Ingolia et al., 2011), our data revealed that only a few of these mRNAs contain uORFs with regulatory properties that significantly enhance translation of their downstream coding sequences upon eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data showing a limited set of translationally upregulated mRNAs.

claim: The stress-induced, uORF-mediated regulation of GCN4 translation in yeast established the paradigm for this mode of regulation.
source: The stress-induced, uORF-mediated regulation of GCN4 translation in yeast established the paradigm for this mode of regulation (Dever et al., 1995; Grant et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Dever et al., 1995; Grant et al., 1995).

claim: In yeast, GCN2 is activated in amino acid-starved yeast by the accumulation of uncharged tRNAs, catalyzing eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: As in mammalian cells, GCN2 is activated in amino acid-starved yeast by the accumulation of uncharged tRNAs, catalyzing eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about GCN2 activation in yeast.

claim: GCN4 is a bZIP transcription factor with homology to mammalian ATF4.
source: The transcript encoding GCN4, a bZIP transcription factor with homology to mammalian ATF4, has four uORFs that modulate translation of its coding sequence upon stress.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about GCN4.

claim: The GCN4 transcript has four uORFs that modulate translation of its coding sequence upon stress.
source: The transcript encoding GCN4, a bZIP transcription factor with homology to mammalian ATF4, has four uORFs that modulate translation of its coding sequence upon stress.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about GCN4 regulation.

claim: GCN4 induction is thought to occur via a re-scanning mechanism that allows 40S ribosomal subunits to remain mRNA-bound after completing the translation of short reading frames and subsequently reinitiate in the downstream coding sequence after reloading with ternary complex.
source: GCN4 induction is thought to occur via a re-scanning mechanism that allows 40S ribosomal subunits to remain mRNA-bound after completing the translation of short reading frames and subsequently reinitiate in the downstream coding sequence after reloading with ternary complex (Hinnebusch, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Hinnebusch, 2005).

claim: The select mRNAs that are translationally upregulated in mammalian cells have uORFs that vary in number, length, and distance from the coding sequences.
source: The select mRNAs that are translationally upregulated in mammalian cells have uORFs that vary in number, length, and distance from the coding sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the identified ISR translational targets.

claim: The uORF2 of ATF4 mRNA showed ribosome density, supporting the notion that it is translated under normal growth conditions.
source: As was observed for GCN4, the uORF2 of ATF4 mRNA showed ribosome density, supporting the notion that it is translated under normal growth conditions (Ingolia et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Ingolia et al., 2009).

claim: The regulation of ISR translational targets depends on their uORFs.
source: Whether the same mechanism of rescanning is utilized by all these mRNAs is not known but, like ATF4, their regulation depends on their uORFs (Vattem and Wek, 2004; Zhou et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009; Palam et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Vattem and Wek, 2004; Zhou et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009; Palam et al., 2011).

claim: Ribosome profiling of HEK293T cells upon arsenite treatment revealed the increased synthesis of SLC35A4.
source: Ribosome profiling of HEK293T cells upon arsenite treatment, a potent inducer of eIF2α phosphorylation, also revealed the increased synthesis of SLC35A4 (Andreev et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Andreev et al., 2015).

claim: SLC35A4 belongs to a large family of nucleotide sugar transporters (NSTs) that are highly conserved transmembrane antiporters localized to the ER or Golgi apparatus.
source: It belongs to a large family of nucleotide sugar transporters (NSTs) that are highly conserved transmembrane antiporters localized to the ER or Golgi apparatus (Song, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Song, 2013).

claim: SLC35A4 may function as the elusive ER-localized UDP-glucose transporter.
source: The role of SLC35A4 in cells is unknown but it may function as the elusive ER-localized UDP-glucose transporter.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the properties of SLC35A4 and its induction during ER stress.

claim: Unfolded ER proteins are continuously de- and re-glucosylated on their N-glycans using UDP-glucose as the glucose donor.
source: This hypothesis is particularly attractive in the context of our data because unfolded ER proteins, which trigger the ISR, are continuously de- and re-glucosylated on their N-glycans using UDP-glucose as the glucose donor.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ER protein folding.

claim: Proteins with monoglucosylated N-glycans bind calnexin or calreticulin which promote protein folding.
source: Proteins with monoglucosylated N-glycans bind calnexin or calreticulin which promote protein folding.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ER protein folding.

claim: Translational induction of SLC35A4 may quickly enhance UDP-glucose transport into the ER lumen upon the accumulation of unfolded proteins in order to promote the pro-folding pathway.
source: Translational induction of SLC35A4 may thus quickly enhance UDP-glucose transport into the ER lumen upon the accumulation of unfolded proteins in order to promote this pro-folding pathway.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the induction of SLC35A4 during ER stress and its putative function.

claim: Ribosome profiling upon activation of the UPR uncovered additional mRNAs induced upon eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Ribosome profiling upon activation of the UPR uncovered additional mRNAs induced upon eIF2α phosphorylation (our data, Reid et al., 2014; Andreev et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data from this study and citations to other studies (Reid et al., 2014; Andreev et al., 2015).

claim: Several ISR-induced translational targets encode for proteins with entirely unknown functions.
source: Several of these mRNAs encode for proteins with entirely unknown functions and the remaining targets are involved in a wide range of cellular processes.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the identified ISR translational targets.

claim: ISRIB blocked the differential translation of ISR-induced translational targets, suggesting that these changes were due to phospho-eIF2α.
source: ISRIB blocked their differential translation, suggesting that these changes were due to phospho-eIF2α.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ISRIB reverses the translational changes.

claim: OPHN1 is a neuron-specific mRNA containing uORFs that is translationally upregulated after mGluR engagement and eIF2α phosphorylation and induces LTD.
source: For example, OPHN1 is a neuron-specific mRNA containing uORFs that is translationally upregulated after mGluR engagement and eIF2α phosphorylation and induces LTD.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about OPHN1.

claim: By blocking the effects of phospho-eIF2α in cells, ISRIB blocks mGluR-dependent LTD.
source: By blocking the effects of phospho-eIF2α in cells, ISRIB also blocks mGluR-dependent LTD (Di Prisco et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Di Prisco et al., 2014).

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation modestly, yet significantly, decreased translation of a large number of ribosomal proteins and elongation factors.
source: The ribosome profiling data presented here revealed that eIF2α phosphorylation modestly, yet significantly, decreased translation of a large number of ribosomal proteins and elongation factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The decrease in translation of ribosomal proteins and elongation factors upon eIF2α phosphorylation is small in magnitude, but its effects on bulk protein synthesis in the cell are significant as these represent a large number of highly expressed proteins.
source: Although the decrease in translation of ribosomal proteins and elongation factors upon eIF2α phosphorylation is small in magnitude, its effects on bulk protein synthesis in the cell are significant as these represent a large number of highly expressed proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the abundance and function of ribosomal proteins and elongation factors.

claim: mTOR regulates translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs via phosphorylation of inhibitory eIF4E-binding proteins.
source: Translation of these mRNAs was previously shown to be under control of mTOR kinase, which regulates mRNA cap-binding factor eIF4E via phosphorylation of inhibitory eIF4E-binding proteins, thereby adjusting protein synthesis in cells in response to the cell's energy and nutrient status (Ma and Blenis, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Ma and Blenis, 2009).

claim: Upon mTOR inhibition, translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs is reduced and the expression of factors required for protein synthesis is diminished.
source: Upon mTOR inhibition, translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs is reduced and the expression of factors required for protein synthesis is diminished.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mTOR regulation.

claim: The observed effect that eIF2α phosphorylation preferentially decreased translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs could be due to inhibition of mTOR in response to ER stress.
source: The observed effect that eIF2α phosphorylation preferentially decreased translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs could, in principle, be due to inhibition of mTOR in response to ER stress.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for the observed effect.

claim: ISRIB reversed the translational changes in 5′ TOP mRNAs, indicating that they are likely to be downstream consequences of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: However, ISRIB reversed the translational changes, indicating that they are likely to be downstream consequences of eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ISRIB reverses the translational changes.

claim: If the translational changes in 5′ TOP mRNAs reflect altered mTOR activity, then the change in mTOR signaling must result from reduced translation mediated by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Thus, if these translational changes do reflect altered mTOR activity, then the change in mTOR signaling must result from reduced translation mediated by eIF2α phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ISRIB reverses the translational changes.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation may lead to silencing of 5′ TOP mRNAs by recruiting them into SGs.
source: Alternatively, eIF2α phosphorylation may lead to silencing of these mRNAs by recruiting them into SGs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an alternative mechanism for the observed effect.

claim: The RNA binding proteins TIA-1 and TIAR bind to TOP mRNAs, leading to their translational downregulation upon amino acid starvation.
source: The RNA binding proteins TIA-1 and TIAR, which are prominently SG-associated, were previously shown to bind to TOP mRNAs, leading to their translational downregulation upon amino acid starvation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about TIA-1 and TIAR.

claim: The effect of TIA-1 and TIAR on TOP mRNA translation required both mTOR inhibition and GCN2 activation.
source: This effect required both mTOR inhibition and GCN2 activation, the latter resulting in eIF2 phosphorylation (Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011).

claim: SGs recruit signaling molecules including upstream negative regulators of mTORC1 (raptor and DYRK3) and mTORC1 itself.
source: SGs also have been shown to recruit signaling molecules including upstream negative regulators of mTORC1 (raptor and DYRK3) and mTORC1 itself, and thus, SG formation may reduce their presence in the cytosol and impede translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs (Thedieck et al., 2013; Wippich et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Thedieck et al., 2013; Wippich et al., 2013).

claim: SG formation may reduce the presence of mTORC1 regulators in the cytosol and impede translation of 5′ TOP mRNAs.

evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism by which SG formation affects 5′ TOP mRNA translation.

claim: The dynamic nature of SGs allowed monitoring of the action of ISRIB upon its addition to live cells in real time.
source: The dynamic nature of SGs allowed us to monitor the action of ISRIB upon its addition to live cells in real time.
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging experiments.

claim: Addition of ISRIB to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs lead to their quick dissolution (less than 5 min).
source: Strikingly, addition of ISRIB to stressed cells with pre-formed SGs lead to their quick dissolution (less than 5 min), liberating mRNAs back into the translational pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data.

claim: A pulse of [35S]-methionine confirmed the fast recovery in protein synthesis even in the presence of stress after ISRIB addition.
source: A pulse of [35S]-methionine confirmed the fast recovery in protein synthesis even in the presence of stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by [35S]-methionine incorporation data.

claim: ISRIB's quick action suggests a direct effect on translation initiation.
source: Although the molecular target of ISRIB remains unknown, its quick action suggests a direct effect on translation initiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rapid kinetics of ISRIB action.

claim: Phospho-eIF2α resistance has been observed both in yeast and in mammalian cells.
source: Phospho-eIF2α resistance has been observed both in yeast and in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In yeast, mutations in eIF2B and eIF5 have been reported to make cells insensitive to eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: In yeast, mutations in eIF2B (the GEF for eIF2) and eIF5 (the 48S PIC-associated GTPase-activating protein for eIF2) have been reported to make cells insensitive to this phosphorylation event (Vazquez de Aldana and Hinnebusch, 1994; Pavitt et al., 1997, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Vazquez de Aldana and Hinnebusch, 1994; Pavitt et al., 1997, 1998).

source: In mammalian cells, TLR4 engagement in macrophages leads to increased eIF2B activity by removal of an inhibitory phosphorylation and insensitivity to ISR activation (Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Woo et al., 2012).

source: SGs contain a large number of RBPs that harbor low complexity sequence domains that nucleate through transient, low affinity interactions (Kato et al., 2012).

claim: A conspicuous feature of some degenerative diseases is the cytoplasmic or nuclear aggregation of RBPs, driven in some cases by pathogenic mutations.

source: TDP-43 and FUS mutations are found in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) (Li et al., 2013), and mutations in hnRNPA1 and hnRPNPA2/B1 have also been found in ALS (Kim et al., 2013).

source: The impact of these cytosolic aggregates on SG dynamics is not known, though they may hamper the ability of SGs to properly dissolve, thereby contributing to sustained translational attenuation and neurodegeneration.
